newsitem.title: ITALY: Dairy farmers ease protests as Italy works out aid.
newsitem.headline: Dairy farmers ease protests as Italy works out aid.

text.p: Italian farmers on Saturday eased their 10-day protest in Milan against huge EU fines for milk overproduction that has brought chaos to the city's main Linate airport, but vowed to fight on until their demands were met.

Farmers agreed to free a stretch of one of the principal road arteries, which they had been blocking with tractors and cars, until Monday when they hope to have a response from the government to their demands.
Milan's prefect (regional governor) Roberto Sorge had earlier ordered the protestors to free at least one carriageway in each direction.
"We will not tolerate other illegal acts," he told reporters. "There can be no more road blocks."

Linate was closed for two hours on Friday because the protests, which have forced passengers to walk at least a kilometre to the terminal, had put the airport's emergency services in jeopardy. Sorge warned that police would be sent in if barriers were not removed.

Some 20 protesters tried to drive into Rome at dawn with their tractors but were thwarted by foggy weather and blocked by police. Rome's prefect Giorgio Musio subsequently banned agricultural vehicles from the roads until Monday.

But there was no sign that the farmers, who have been hit with some 370 billion lire ($230 million) of fines to be paid by the end of this month for exceeding strict European Union milk quotas, were giving up. Other protests were still in progress in Venice and the southern city of Taranto.
"We will continue our protests in a peaceful way...until we get what we want," said one demonstrator in Milan.
Italian dairy farmers want the government to pay the levies, but Prime Minister Romano Prodi has refused, offering cheap loans instead.

The Agriculture Ministry maintained in a statement on Saturday that farmers would be responsible for the fines themselves but said it would ask the EU to allow farmers to pay to pay a first instalment by the end of January.

The Agriculture Ministry said on Saturday that farmers would be eligible for five-year loans up to a maximum of 350 billion lire ($220,000 ) carrying interest rates of less than three percent and other measures to compensate for loss of income. ($1=1597 Lire)
